The post A million samples, 52,000 people, and a new view of disease appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> A Mayo Clinic Biobank team member works with samples stored in cryogenic tanks for use in research.
Mayo Clinic's Biobank is enabling discovery on a new scale as genomic data from 52,000 participants can be studied alongside medical records, imaging, pathology and a growing body of research data across Mayo Clinic.
Inside Mayo Clinic's Marvin Building, Janet Olson, Ph.D., walks past rows of freezers containing more than 1 million tubes of biological samples donated for research to the Mayo Clinic Biobank. The collection she helped develop starting in 2009 has supported more than 650 studies spanning heart disease, cancer, neurological disorders and many other conditions.
Janet Olson, Ph.D.
Now, advances in genomic sequencing and analysis have made it possible to read those samples in extraordinary new ways. Researchers have analyzed the protein-coding regions of DNA from all 52,000 participants, identifying genetic changes linked to disease.
The findings add a new layer to the health information participants have contributed over the years, giving researchers a richer view of how genetics may influence health. The genomic data have also become part of a much larger research resource: Mayo Clinic’s Research Data Atlas, which brings together more than 6,000 research datasets.
"This is beyond the scope of what we even imagined when we started the Biobank," says Dr. Olson, an epidemiologist and principal investigator of the Biobank. "We never would have dreamed that this kind of research would be possible at this scale."
Watch: Dr. Janet Olson discusses the Biobank: Videography by Kevin Sullivan, Mayo Clinic
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:40) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Connecting the Biobank to a broader research ecosystem
The genetic data have become even more revealing when viewed alongside what happened to participants over time. Biobank participants consented to have their samples studied alongside their Mayo Clinic medical records, allowing researchers to connect genetic risk with years of health history.
"One of our strengths is our medical record and how deep our medical records are," Dr. Olson says. "There are patients that we have data from the time they were born."
The Biobank's genomic data can now be studied alongside thousands of other datasets in the Research Data Atlas, including clinical, imaging, pathology and other research data. That gives researchers a way to examine connections across large groups of people and across different aspects of human biology.
An automated laboratory system processes biological samples inside the Mayo Clinic Biobank.
Artificial intelligence can help researchers search those vast collections of information for relationships that might be difficult to spot otherwise. Such analyses could help researchers better understand how disease develops, identify people at greater risk and explore why the same disease can take different paths.
Uncovering hidden genetic risk in nearly 2,500 participants
The growing ability to understand genetic risk is also creating opportunities to return potentially important findings to the people who made the research possible.
Large-scale genomic analysis has identified about 2,500 participants with potentially medically actionable findings, including inherited risks for serious cancers and cardiovascular diseases. Over 1,000 have been offered the opportunity to receive their results, leading some of them to clinical confirmation, additional testing, surveillance or specialty care. Genetic counselors help participants decide whether they want to learn the result and, if they do, arrange confirmatory clinical testing and follow-up care.
Related Story: A shattered leg, a blood sample and a discovery that may have saved a family
A Mayo Clinic Biobank sample led to the discovery of a rare inherited mutation in Chad Rockow and three family members.
"Ten years ago, only a fraction of the things that are now being returned were returnable," Dr. Olson says. "As more and more knowledge is gained, more and more patients are going to have results that are returnable."
A research resource built for future discoveries
Long before "biobank" became a familiar term, Dr. Olson was helping build one. She and her colleague, Fergus Couch, Ph.D., established one of Mayo Clinic's early biobanking resources through the Mayo Clinic Breast Cancer Study. The collection brought together blood samples and health information from approximately 10,000 women with breast cancer.
That resource has enabled collaborations with researchers across the globe and contributed to important discoveries through the Breast Cancer Association Consortium (BCAC), CARRIERS (Cancer Risk Estimates Related to Susceptibility), and the Triple Negative Breast Cancer Consortium.
Dr. Olson calls genomic data a "renewable resource" because the same genetic information can be studied again and again without using up the original sample. Preserving physical specimens means researchers can return to them as new technologies emerge, sometimes uncovering biological information that could not be measured when the samples were first collected. In this way, biobanking allows samples donated today to continue supporting discoveries well into the future.
She is applying that thinking to Mayo Clinic's next generation of research, advising a collection envisioned to eventually include as many as 1 million participants and contributing to Precure Research, a Mayo Clinic initiative which is building cohorts to study biological changes before illness becomes clinically apparent.
"We're always aware that samples that we collect, we're going to set aside a portion, so that when the technology comes along, we have the samples ready," Dr. Olson says.
For Dr. Olson, the Biobank's greatest significance lies in the people behind it: Every sample carries the trust of someone who chose to help science move forward for someone else.
The bigger picture
This research aligns with Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative, which focuses on developing tools and approaches to identify disease-related risk earlier, before symptoms emerge or conditions become more difficult to treat. Visit mayo.edu/research/precure for more information.

The post Checkpoint immunotherapy reshapes immune environment in lymph nodes appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Jessica Lancaster, Ph.D., Mayo Clinic immunologist, places a sample into a light-sheet microscope as a colleague works behind her.
PHOENIX — A new study from Mayo Clinic suggests checkpoint immunotherapy may reshape the immune environment within lymph nodes after melanoma has spread to them. Researchers found that treatment reorganized several types of immune cells and changed the behavior of certain cells, called macrophages, that can either support or suppress an immune response depending on their environment.
Checkpoint immunotherapy helps the immune system recognize and attack cancer by blocking signals that can restrain immune cells. While these treatments have transformed cancer care, not all patients benefit, and researchers are working to understand why responses vary.
The study, published in Communications Biology, could help answer that question. The findings suggest that how immunotherapy reshapes the lymph node environment — not just how it affects individual immune cells — may be an important part of the body's response to treatment.
"We're learning that treating cancer isn't only about the T cells themselves. We also have to think about the environment they're working in," says Jessica Lancaster, Ph.D., senior author of the study and a Mayo Clinic immunologist. "Our study suggests that you may need to renovate the entire neighborhood to create an effective antitumor response."
Looking beyond T cells
That neighborhood includes the lymph nodes, which are organized hubs where immune cells interact and immune responses begin. Lymph nodes also can be among the first places melanoma spreads.
Using a preclinical model of melanoma metastasis, Mayo Clinic researchers studied lymph nodes that drain the area around a tumor following checkpoint immunotherapy. They combined advanced imaging with cellular and gene-expression analyses to examine which cells were present, where they were located and how they changed with treatment.
Treatment reduced the amount of metastatic tumor in the lymph nodes and reorganized T cells, B cells, myeloid cells and cells that provide the lymph node's structural framework.
Researchers saw particularly notable changes in macrophages, immune cells that normally help clear damaged and dying cells but can be influenced by tumors to suppress the immune response.
After checkpoint immunotherapy, macrophages showed signs of shifting toward a more immune-stimulating state. Researchers also observed greater physical separation between macrophages and T cells, which may reduce suppressive interactions.
The work builds on Mayo Clinic's long-standing research into immune checkpoints. Dr. Lancaster's team collaborated with Haidong Dong, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic cancer immunology researcher whose earlier work contributed to understanding the checkpoint pathway targeted in this study.
"For years, much of the focus has been on how these treatments help T cells attack cancer. What's been missing from the big picture is the role of myeloid cells," Dr. Dong says. "This study shows that these cells can also be reprogrammed to help stimulate the immune response against cancer."
A broader view of immunotherapy
The findings suggest that effective immunotherapy may depend not only on activating T cells but also on creating an environment where different immune cells can work together against cancer.
"The lymph node is the site of immune activation," Dr. Lancaster says. "Understanding what happens there could help us think differently about how to design therapies for different types of cancer."
The researchers caution that the study was conducted in a preclinical model and does not fully replicate how melanoma develops and spreads in people. Future studies will be needed to determine whether the same immune changes occur in patients and how they relate to treatment response.
The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, the Miltenyi Biotec Spatial Biology Award, David F. and Margaret T. Grohne Cancer Immunology and Immunotherapeutics Research Program within Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, Mayo Clinic Breast Cancer Specialized Program of Research Excellence (SPORE) and Mayo Clinic Hepatobiliary Cancer SPORE.
For a complete list of authors, disclosures and funding, review the study.

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Mayo Clinic researchers have found that genetic testing can help identify people who carry inherited blood disorder traits, including individuals who may not otherwise know their carrier status. Earlier identification can create opportunities for genetic counseling, informed family planning and appropriate clinical follow-up.
Using genetic data from nearly 50,000 participants, Mayo Clinic researchers identified carrier traits for sickle cell anemia and beta-thalassemia at clinically significant levels. Published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, the study shows how population-scale genetic testing may complement existing screening approaches and provide patients and clinicians with additional information about inherited health risks.
Nathaniel Miller, M.D.
"If we can identify carrier status earlier, we have more opportunities for reproductive counseling, appropriate preventive care and helping patients understand what these findings may mean for their families," says Nathaniel Miller, M.D., a Mayo Clinic family medicine physician and first author of the study, published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.
Screening practices have evolved over time. All U.S. states screen newborns for clinically significant hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease, but practices for identifying and reporting carrier status have varied, particularly for thalassemias. Some adults also were born before comparable newborn screening was available. The findings illustrate how genetic testing later in life may provide health information that was not available earlier.
Genetic testing provides additional insight into carrier status
Sickle cell anemia and beta-thalassemia are hemoglobinopathies — inherited disorders that affect hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body. In sickle cell anemia, abnormal hemoglobin causes some red blood cells to become rigid, sticky and misshapen, which can slow or block blood flow. Beta-thalassemia reduces the body's production of hemoglobin and can lead to anemia. People with sickle cell trait or beta-thalassemia trait often have few or no symptoms, but they can pass the genetic change to their children.
The research used data from Tapestry, which enrolled more than 98,000 participants across Mayo Clinic between July 2020 and May 2024. The initiative generated whole exome sequencing data to support clinical care, research discovery and genomic education. Researchers analyzed genetic data from nearly 50,000 participants for variants associated with sickle cell trait and beta-thalassemia trait and compared those findings with diagnosis codes in participants' electronic health records.
Among 116 participants identified through genetic testing with sickle cell trait, 19 had a corresponding diagnosis code. Among 98 participants identified as carriers of beta-thalassemia, 47 had a corresponding diagnosis code. The differences illustrate how genetic testing can add information to a person's health history, particularly when carrier status may not have been identified through earlier screening. Researchers also found instances in which existing diagnosis codes did not correspond with the genetic findings. The authors say additional research is needed to understand these differences, which may reflect variations in historical screening, classification and documentation practices.
Moving toward earlier identification
The findings point to opportunities to develop clearer guidance for identifying hemoglobinopathy carrier status and determining when genetic testing and counseling may be appropriate. Primary care clinicians may be particularly well positioned to help identify people who could benefit from testing before pregnancy.
Isa Houwink, M.D., Ph.D.
"From a primary care and population health perspective, the goal is to identify carrier status early, ideally before pregnancy, because many people don't know they are carriers," says Isa Houwink, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic family medicine physician and senior author of the study. "That creates an important opportunity for preconception counseling and informed family planning."
The research aligns with Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative, which focuses on developing tools and approaches to identify disease-related risk earlier, before symptoms emerge or conditions become more difficult to treat. Visit mayo.edu/research/precure for more information.

PHOENIX — Mayo Clinic researchers have detected measurable changes in the brain within 18 minutes of deep brain stimulation (DBS) in people with drug-resistant epilepsy, a finding that could eventually help clinicians personalize treatment without waiting months to determine whether stimulation settings are effective. The study was recently published in iScience.
DBS is approved by the Food and Drug Administration as a therapy for certain patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. Electrical pulses delivered through electrodes implanted in the brain can help reduce seizures. But finding the most effective stimulation settings can require months or even years of adjustments.
Jonathon Parker, M.D., Ph.D.
"One of the biggest questions we have when we stimulate the brain with therapeutic devices is: Are these the right settings for the person sitting across from me?" says Jonathon Parker, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurosurgeon in Arizona and senior author of the study. "Right now, we may have to wait months to see whether a patient's seizures improve. We're trying to find a brain signal that could eventually give us that information much earlier."
Listening to the brain's response
The study included nine adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy who were undergoing intracranial electroencephalogram (EEG) monitoring at Mayo Clinic as part of their clinical care. Researchers examined how communication between the thalamus and other areas of the brain changed before and after short periods of stimulation.
They compared two stimulation patterns, which Dr. Parker likens to the difference between two drummers. Conventional stimulation resembles a drumline playing a steady, predictable beat. Nonperiodic stimulation is more like a jazz drummer, with beats arriving at less predictable intervals.
Researchers found that the two stimulation patterns affected brain communication differently. Those changes were particularly evident in the connections between the thalamus and areas of the brain's frontal lobe.
"That was one of our aha moments," Dr. Parker says. "Different stimulation patterns can change the way the thalamus communicates with other areas of the brain. The brain is telling us something when we stimulate it. We're developing the tools to understand if that response can predict future reduction of seizures."
From months of waiting to measurable signals
For epilepsy, determining whether DBS is effective can be particularly challenging. Seizure reduction can take months to emerge, and seizures occur intermittently, making it difficult to assess treatment success soon after stimulation settings are changed.
The findings suggest that measurable changes in brain connectivity may provide an earlier, objective signal of how the brain is responding to stimulation.
Researchers say the next step is to determine whether the brain responses they measured are associated with long-term seizure reduction and clinical improvement.
The Mayo Clinic team has expanded this research beyond the nine participants in the published study and is investigating whether information gathered could eventually be captured using less invasive methods.
"The goal is to take what we can learn from these very highly precise recordings and determine the minimum amount of information we need to understand the brain's response to stimulation," Dr. Parker says. "Ultimately, we want to translate this measurement into something noninvasive and useful to clinicians and patients."
Researchers are also exploring how machine learning and artificial intelligence could help clinicians interpret brain signals and guide stimulation settings. Any predictive algorithms would require prospective validation before clinical use, Dr. Parker notes.
Patients make the research possible
Dr. Parker credits the patients with drug-resistant epilepsy who volunteered for the study while undergoing invasive brain monitoring.
"The patients are the true heroes," he says. "They're volunteering their time to be part of these studies and helping create a path toward better care for patients in the future."
The research was funded in part by funds from the Neurosurgery Research and Education Foundation (NREF).

Standing in a laboratory amid technologies capable of probing human biology at extraordinary scale and depth, Konstantinos Lazaridis, M.D., is leading Mayo Clinic's effort to understand the exposome — the totality of environmental exposures that can influence human health.
The exposome is, in many ways, a record of a life lived — the air someone breathes, the food and water they consume, the environments they inhabit, and countless other influences that can leave a biological imprint and interact with a person's genes.
Dr. Lazaridis and his colleagues are calling for exposome research to match the scope and rigor of the Human Genome Project. He and his colleagues lay out what that will take in a new Mayo Clinic Proceedings special article, "The Exposome and Its Impact on Health and Disease."
"Genomics changed medicine by giving us the first complete picture of our DNA sequence and revealing the genetic roots of disease," says Dr. Lazaridis, the Carlson and Nelson Endowed Executive Director of Mayo Clinic's Center for Individualized Medicine. "I believe we are entering another moment of that magnitude."
Watch: Dr. Konstantinos Lazaridis discusses the exposome:
Videography by Kevin Sullivan, Mayo Clinic
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (2:53) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Understanding the exposome
Scientists now have new tools to measure the exposome. Advances in molecular science, wearable devices, geolocation records and artificial intelligence are making it possible to study environmental exposures at a scale that was not previously possible.
The exposome includes chemicals in air, water and food, pesticides, heavy metals, microplastics, diet, traffic noise, nighttime light pollution, and more. Dr. Lazaridis and his colleagues point to studies linking lead exposure with fatty liver disease, traffic noise with atrial fibrillation, air pollution with declining kidney function and nighttime light pollution with Alzheimer's disease.
The exposome also includes social factors such as isolation, loneliness, social support and neighborhood connections. Not all exposures are harmful. Potentially beneficial exposures include physical activity, restorative sleep, green space, a healthy diet, vitamins, micronutrients and compounds found in tea and coffee.
"Disease doesn't happen in a vacuum," Dr. Lazaridis says. "We are born with our genome, but we also live in an environment that affects how we develop, how we age and what diseases we may face."
The challenge is that exposures rarely occur one at a time. Their effects can combine and accumulate over decades, while some exposures are difficult to capture at all. Certain chemicals leave the body quickly and may no longer be detectable even after triggering a biological response.
How Precure Research will study environmental exposures
Inside Mayo Clinic’s Kellen Building, a center for biomedical research and innovation, researchers use advanced laboratory tools to explore the biological processes that shape human health and disease.
Mayo Clinic is building the infrastructure to study the exposome through Precure Research, which Dr. Lazaridis directs. The initiative aims to detect the earliest shifts in disease biology — long before symptoms appear — when intervention may still be possible. Its initial focus spans the brain, heart, kidneys, liver and lungs, where researchers are looking for shared biological themes, including inflammation, aging and environmental influences.
Researchers will measure exposures in blood and urine and track how the body responds. Combined with clinical and genomic information, the research could generate billions or trillions of data points, with artificial intelligence helping researchers find patterns across large populations. That scale brings an equally large responsibility, Dr. Lazaridis says, and the research is being conducted with safeguards to protect privacy and ensure scientific rigor.
Heavy metals such as arsenic and lead will be among the first exposures the team studies, including the effects of long-term exposure at moderate levels. One question is whether lower levels of lead exposure may play a role in fatty liver disease.
Researchers will analyze blood, urine, stool and saliva, expanding the work to pesticides, xenobiotics, and other environmental chemicals. As measurement methods advance, the team also plans to study microplastics and nanoplastics.
Geolocation data will help researchers compare environmental conditions where people live with exposures over time measured in the body.
"If you live close to a major highway compared with a farm, you probably have different exposures," Dr. Lazaridis says. "We want to see whether the exposures we measure in the body match what we know about the surrounding environment."
How environmental exposures may affect treatment
A researcher examines biological samples with an advanced imaging system in a Kellen Building laboratory at Mayo Clinic.
Mayo Clinic researchers are also applying exposome science to another fundamental question: Why can the same medication affect people differently? Mayo Clinic is part of a federally funded, seven-institution project studying how environmental exposures may affect the impact of diabetes medications.
Researchers are measuring exposures in blood to determine whether they influence genes and proteins involved in drug metabolism. The goal is to understand why diabetes medications work differently for different people in ways that genetics alone may not explain.
Unlike inherited DNA that cannot be altered, some environmental risks may be reduced or avoided. If researchers can identify exposures that contribute to disease and detect their effects early, clinicians may have a chance to act before disease develops or damage becomes irreversible. "I can see the day when we meet with patients and talk about exposures in a very specific way — which ones may be affecting their health and where there may be an opportunity to intervene," Dr. Lazaridis says.
A front-row seat to two scientific revolutions
Researchers work at laboratory benches in Mayo Clinic’s Kellen Building, using precision tools to prepare and process samples.
Inside the laboratory, Dr. Lazaridis describes how exposome research could move from scientific discovery toward patient care: start with a sample, find a signal, uncover the mechanism and determine whether it can make a clinical difference.
Earlier in his career, Dr. Lazaridis worked in genomics at the National Institutes of Health as the Human Genome Project was underway. He had a firsthand view of a scientific revolution that opened an extraordinary new window into human disease.
Now, with the exposome, he is helping Mayo Clinic push open another.
The bigger picture
The work aligns with Mayo Clinic’s Precure Research, which focuses on identifying disease risk earlier and creating opportunities to intervene sooner. For exposome research, that means understanding how environmental exposures influence disease biology and finding ways to detect those effects before disease develops. Visit mayo.edu/research/precure for more information.

ROCHESTER, Minn., and PHOENIX — A Mayo Clinic study published in the Journal of Neuro-Oncology suggests that analyzing DNA in cerebrospinal fluid could provide another source of information when MRI cannot provide a clear brain tumor diagnosis or obtaining tissue through biopsy is difficult or potentially unsafe.
The study included 76 patients facing one of three challenging clinical scenarios:
An abnormality in the brain or spinal cord without a diagnosis;
Imaging changes that could reflect either tumor growth or treatment effects; or
Suspected leptomeningeal disease, in which cancer spreads to the membranes and fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
The investigation detected tumor-associated DNA in 20 patients (26%). For those patients, the findings provided another piece of evidence that clinicians could consider alongside imaging, pathology and the patient's overall clinical picture.
Why can MRI and tissue biopsy leave unanswered questions in brain tumor care?
MRI and tissue biopsy remain essential for diagnosing and monitoring cancers involving the brain and spinal cord. But each has limitations.
Changes on an MRI can often look similar whether they are caused by cancer, inflammation or the effects of treatment. In other cases, a lesion's location may make obtaining tissue through biopsy difficult or unsafe.
Researchers are increasingly studying whether tumor-related material released into body fluids can provide another source of information. A liquid biopsy looks for material such as tumor DNA in a body fluid rather than in a tissue sample. Most liquid biopsies use blood.
For brain tumors, however, the blood-brain barrier — a protective boundary that controls what passes between the bloodstream and the brain — can limit how much tumor DNA reaches the bloodstream, making it difficult to detect.
Mayo Clinic researchers are therefore studying cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, the clear fluid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord. Tumor cells can release small DNA fragments into this fluid. These fragments, known as cell-free DNA, may contain genetic changes associated with a tumor.
Terry Burns, M.D., Ph.D.
CSF can be collected through a lumbar puncture, also known as a spinal tap, in which a thin needle is inserted into the lower back. Researchers then analyze the DNA fragments in the sample for changes in individual genes and broader DNA patterns associated with tumors.
"In some cases, this CSF DNA approach has provided important diagnostic information when obtaining tissue safely was not an option," says Terry Burns, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurosurgeon and senior author of the study.
What did Mayo Clinic researchers find in CSF?
Patients in this study represented three clinical groups:
35 had a brain or spinal cord abnormality whose cause was uncertain;
21 had imaging changes that could represent either tumor progression or treatment-related effects; and
20 were being evaluated for leptomeningeal disease
Across the 76 patients, the analysis found signs of tumor DNA in 20 patients. In 29 patients, the samples contained enough DNA for analysis, but no signs of tumor DNA were detected. The remaining 27 samples did not contain enough usable DNA to complete the analysis.
A negative result did not rule out cancer. The amount of tumor DNA in CSF can vary, and some samples may contain too little tumor DNA for the analysis to detect. Researchers are working to improve the analysis of samples containing very small amounts of DNA.
How could CSF DNA testing inform brain tumor care?
Analyzing cell-free DNA in CSF could provide more than a sign that tumor material is present. The DNA fragments may also contain information about a tumor's genetic features. In the future, that information could help care teams identify clinical trials or treatments that target specific genetic changes.
The test used in this study remains investigational. When it can be obtained safely, tumor tissue remains the gold standard for making a definitive diagnosis. Researchers are working to determine which patients may benefit most from CSF DNA analysis and when the approach could add useful information to imaging, pathology and other established methods.
Cecile Riviere-Cazaux
"Our goal is for CSF cell-free DNA testing to provide patients and their care teams with diagnostic insights when answers may otherwise be difficult to obtain," says Cecile Riviere-Cazaux, a Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine student in Rochester and co-first author of the study. "As we gain more experience, we hope it will also help connect patients with clinical trials and personalized treatment options."
Mayo Clinic researchers are now working to improve the analysis of samples containing very small amounts of tumor DNA and to determine how changes in DNA and other biomarkers over time could help show whether a tumor is responding to treatment.

ROCHESTER, Minn. — An investigational vaccine helped the immune system recognize and respond to mutations that drive most pancreatic cancers, according to results from a randomized phase 2 clinical trial led by Mayo Clinic researchers. The findings, published in Nature Medicine, will help researchers design a larger phase 3 clinical trial.
Nearly every patient evaluated after receiving the vaccine developed an immune response against mutated KRAS, a gene that plays a major role in pancreatic cancer. Mayo Clinic researchers also found that patients with stronger immune responses tended to remain free of disease longer.
"Historically, pancreatic cancer has been very difficult to treat with immunotherapy," says Ben George, M.B.B.S, M.D., a Mayo Clinic medical oncologist and lead author of the study. "What is encouraging is that we were able to generate a strong immune response against KRAS mutations in nearly every patient we evaluated. In an exploratory analysis, patients with greater immune responses to the vaccine appeared protected with longer disease-free survival times.”
Teaching the immune system what to attack
Pancreatic cancer has a high risk of returning even after surgery and chemotherapy. Researchers have been looking for new ways to find and destroy cancer cells that may remain in the body after treatment.
KRAS offers one possible target.
Mutations in the KRAS gene are found in about 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, the most common type of pancreatic cancer. These mutations help cancer cells grow and survive.
The investigational vaccine targets seven of the most common KRAS mutations. It is designed to travel to the lymph nodes, where many immune responses begin. There, the vaccine helps T cells — which are immune cells that can recognize and attack altered cells — to identify cancer cells with mutated KRAS.
Unlike some cancer vaccines made specifically for an individual patient, this vaccine is "off the shelf" and designed for patients whose tumors have one of the KRAS mutations it targets.
The study included 144 patients with stage 1-3 KRAS-mutated pancreatic cancer. All had undergone surgery and chemotherapy and had no cancer visible on imaging when they entered the trial.
Researchers randomly assigned 96 patients to receive the vaccine and 48 to observation.
Strong immune response, but more study is needed
The trial did not meet its primary goal of showing an improvement in disease-free survival across the full study population.
Median disease-free survival, or the length of time patients lived without their cancer returning, was 23.8 months for patients who received the vaccine and 21.2 months for those in the observation group. The difference was not statistically significant.
Researchers found other signals that warrant further study.
Of the 90 patients who received the vaccine and could be evaluated for immune response, 89, or 98.9%, developed increased T-cell responses against mutated KRAS.
Researchers also found an association between the strength of the immune response and how long patients remained free of disease. More than 8 in 10 patients who were able to be evaluated developed a KRAS-specific T-cell response that was more than 9 times greater than before vaccination. Patients who reached that level had longer disease-free survival than those who did not.
"The immune response is an important signal that helps us understand what is happening biologically and gives us important information for the next trial," Dr. George says.
Clues about who may benefit
Researchers also found clues that may help predict which patients are more likely to benefit from the vaccine.
One clue involved circulating tumor DNA, or ctDNA. These are small pieces of DNA released by cancer cells into the bloodstream. Detecting ctDNA after cancer treatment can be a sign that cancer remains in the body even when it cannot be seen on imaging.
In a planned analysis, patients who did not have detectable ctDNA at the start of the study showed a signal of longer disease-free survival with the vaccine compared with observation.
Researchers saw another difference based on whether patients had previously received radiation therapy.
Patients who had received radiation had fewer lymphocytes, a type of white blood cell important to the immune system. They also developed weaker KRAS-specific immune responses after receiving the vaccine. Among patients who had not received radiation, researchers saw a signal of longer disease-free survival with the vaccine.
These findings do not establish which patients will benefit from the vaccine. They do, however, give researchers information to test in a larger trial.
"One of the most useful things we can learn from a phase 2 trial is why patients may respond differently," Dr. George says. "We can take those lessons and design the next study to better answer the question that matters most: Can this approach help patients live longer without their pancreatic cancer returning?"
Building an immune response against cancer
Researchers found that the vaccine activated two important types of T cells, known as CD4 and CD8 T cells. It also produced immune responses against several KRAS mutations.
In a small group of patients, researchers observed another potentially important effect. After vaccination, the immune system began recognizing other cancer-related targets that were not included in the vaccine, a phenomenon researchers call antigen spreading.
The immune response also persisted over time. Among patients who could be evaluated at least 46 weeks after the start of the study, 95.5% still had a detectable KRAS-specific T-cell response.
Researchers say longer follow-up and a larger study are needed. Overall survival results are not yet available, and some findings linking immune response with disease-free survival came from exploratory analyses.
A phase 3 clinical trial is planned to further study whether the vaccine can delay or prevent pancreatic cancer from returning.
"We've shown that we can teach the immune system to recognize these KRAS mutations," Dr. George says. "The next step is finding out whether doing that can change the course of the disease for patients."

The post Easing migraine-related light sensitivity with the right kind of white light appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Weather changes in the fall and spring can trigger migraine headaches, according to the American Migraine Foundation, which estimates that about 40 million Americans and 1 billion people worldwide live with this type of debilitating headache. Sensitivity to light, also known as photophobia, is one of the most common migraine symptoms. Now, Mayo Clinic researchers and collaborators report that both the brightness and color spectrum of indoor white light may affect how uncomfortable light feels for people with migraine.
https://youtu.be/AkG9-eY9PF4
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video of Dr. Todd Schwedt is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network.
"During a migraine, exposure to normal lighting causes visual discomfort," says Dr. Todd Schwedt, a neurologist at Mayo Clinic in Arizona. "It also worsens the intensity of the migraine headache, often resulting in the need to retreat to a dark room."
In a study published in Sage Journals, researchers from Mayo Clinic and Arizona State University analyzed adults ages 18 to 45 who experienced episodic migraine, reporting four to 14 headache days per month and light sensitivity. Each participant completed two laboratory sessions, one while headache-free and another during an untreated migraine attack.
Participants were exposed to four types of white light enriched with different portions of the visible spectrum: green, blue, cyan and red. The light still appeared white, an important distinction from earlier studies that investigated visibly green light. During testing, researchers gradually increased the brightness. Participants rated their visual discomfort and researchers measured pupil size as an objective indicator of light sensitivity.
As expected, visual discomfort was worse during a migraine attack and with higher intensity light. Investigators also found that green-enriched white light was the most comfortable.
Other key findings:
Green-enriched white light was associated with a 20% to 30% or greater reduction in visual discomfort compared with blue-enriched white light, depending on whether participants were experiencing a migraine attack.
Green-enriched white light was associated with larger pupils and less discomfort, while blue and cyan-enriched light were associated with greater discomfort and smaller pupils.
A second published study demonstrated a 37% reduction in visual discomfort with green-enriched white light and showed that, unlike other lighting, green-enriched white light does not worsen migraine headache intensity.
Researchers were able to develop a special type of white light enriched with green wavelengths that not only reduces visual discomfort and headache intensity but also improves thinking and concentration.
"Optimized lighting can provide more migraine-friendly environments in the workplace, schools, healthcare settings and in homes," says Dr. Schwedt, a co-author of the study. "Because the light still appears white, spectrally tuned lighting can be incorporated into these settings, even when they are shared by people with migraine and light sensitivity and those without."
Researchers are currently investigating potential benefits with longer exposure in real-world settings and whether changes in lighting improve headache severity and frequency and reduce disability.
Dr. Schwedt is a co-founder of Allevalux, a company focused on lighting technology. For a complete list of authors, funding and disclosures, see the study.

The post AI tool may support dermatologists in assessing skin lesions for cancer risk appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> ROCHESTER, Minn. — Mayo Clinic researchers have found that an artificial intelligence (AI) tool may provide dermatologists with additional information to help assess whether skin lesions are cancerous and inform their clinical decisions about whether to biopsy or monitor them, according to a study published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings.
The tool, called Dermoscopy Explainable Intelligence (DEXI), is part of an advanced imaging system that dermatologists use to capture and track skin lesions over time. DEXI assigns lesions a score from 0.0 to 10.0 based on image characteristics associated with cancer risk. It also identifies features — such as asymmetry, border and color — that contribute to the score, providing dermatologists with additional information they can consider alongside their clinical evaluation.
Researchers evaluated DEXI scores for skin lesions with known diagnoses. Using a threshold of 3.0 — meaning a score of 3.0 or higher was considered positive for potential skin cancer — DEXI correctly identified 93.4% of cancerous lesions and 75% of noncancerous lesions.
Left: The image is of a non-cancerous skin lesion with a low-risk DEXI score of 1.2 and reassuring features (asymmetry, border, color and diameter) that help inform physicians that it should be monitored. Right: The image of an invasive melanoma with a high-risk DEXI score of 8.9 and features (asymmetry, border, color and diameter) that help inform physicians that it should be biopsied.
"Prior to the study, I would review a patient's DEXI score, but I wouldn't know exactly what to do with the number," says Jenny Link, M.D., dermatologist at Mayo Clinic and the study's lead author. "Now I can confidently use the score as another piece of data to inform my clinical judgment on whether I recommend a biopsy or monitoring."
Study evaluates DEXI's clinical use
DEXI is a deep-learning tool trained on more than 66,000 annotated dermoscopy images. In addition to assigning a cancer risk score, the tool uses explainable AI to indicate which image features contributed to its score.
The retrospective study included 178 patients who underwent total-body photography, sequential digital dermoscopy imaging and subsequent biopsy of one or more skin lesions.
Researchers analyzed 261 lesions with both a DEXI score and a diagnosis confirmed by tissue examination. They compared scores for noncancerous and cancerous lesions and further separated cancerous lesions into melanoma and nonmelanoma skin cancers.
The average DEXI score was 2.5 for noncancerous lesions, compared with 7.8 for nonmelanoma skin cancers and 6.0 for melanomas. Cancerous lesions had significantly higher DEXI scores than noncancerous lesions. Based on these findings, researchers identified 3.0 as a potential threshold that could help inform clinicians' decisions about monitoring or biopsy.
"We identified 3.0 as a potential DEXI score threshold that could provide useful information when dermatologists are considering whether to monitor a lesion or perform a biopsy," says Dr. Link.
The researchers also identified limitations. DEXI does not account for patient-specific factors, such as age, medications and history of melanoma. The tool was also less effective at evaluating severely atypical nevi, or skin moles, and early evolving melanomas.
"Our study demonstrated that DEXI is a useful and valuable tool to support clinicians as they evaluate cancerous and noncancerous skin lesions, but it should not be used in isolation. The score must be interpreted alongside clinical findings and patient-specific factors, and the tool requires further validation and refinement," says Dr. Link.

ROCHESTER, Minn. — Mayo Clinic researchers are studying whether low-dose radiation therapy can slow the progression of Parkinson's disease by targeting inflammation in areas of the brain affected by the disease.
The clinical trial is the first to investigate low-dose radiation as an anti-inflammatory approach in patients with early-stage Parkinson's disease.
Radiation therapy is most often used to treat cancer, where higher doses are used to damage tumor cells and stop them from growing. In this clinical trial, researchers are taking a very different approach. They are studying whether much lower, targeted doses of radiation can lower inflammation.
"Inflammation is believed to play an important role in the disease process in Parkinson's," says Yasamin Sharifzadeh, M.D., a Mayo Clinic radiation oncologist and principal investigator of the clinical trial. "Instead of treating the symptoms patients experience, we're investigating whether low-dose radiation can affect one of the underlying biological processes associated with the disease and therefore slow the worsening of symptoms."
Why researchers are studying inflammation in Parkinson's disease
Parkinson's disease is a movement disorder of the nervous system that worsens over time. It can cause slowed movement, tremors, muscle stiffness, and problems with balance and posture. Patients also can experience cognitive changes, fatigue, depression and anxiety. The disease is associated with the gradual loss of brain cells that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps control movement, and the buildup of abnormal proteins in and around brain cells.
There is no cure for Parkinson's disease. Treatments focus on managing symptoms with medications and, for some patients, procedures such as focused ultrasound or deep brain stimulation. Researchers continue to study the causes of Parkinson’s disease and what drives its progression.
"Parkinson's disease is not a single uniform condition but rather a collection of related disease subtypes that may differ biologically," says Rodolfo Savica, M.D., Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic neurologist and study investigator. "This diversity complicates the search for a universal treatment, but despite this complication, inflammation appears to play a meaningful role across many forms of the disease."
How the low-dose radiation clinical trial works
In the trial, researchers deliver low-dose radiation to small, carefully targeted areas of the brain believed to be involved in the development and progression of Parkinson's disease. The treatment is limited to specific areas rather than exposing the entire brain to radiation.
"This is very different from using radiation to damage or destroy tissue," explains Dr. Sharifzadeh. "We're using a much lower dose. The goal is not to destroy brain tissue but to investigate whether radiation can reduce inflammatory processes in specific parts of the brain."
Before treatment, researchers use brain imaging to map each participant's anatomy and plan where to deliver the radiation. They also collect blood samples to measure biomarkers and assess participants' physical, cognitive and emotional symptoms.
Participants receive one low-dose radiation treatment a day for five consecutive days. Each treatment lasts about 10 to 15 minutes.
Researchers evaluate changes in inflammatory biomarkers and protein accumulation at six hours after treatment and again at three, six and 12 months. They also use imaging to assess dopamine loss and track participants' physical, cognitive and emotional symptoms throughout the study.
The study includes patients ages 45 to 75 with early-stage Parkinson's disease that is not associated with a known genetic cause. Researchers plan to enroll 20 participants. The clinical trial is available by invitation only at Mayo Clinic in Rochester.
"Parkinson's disease is multifaceted, and there is still much we are learning about the role inflammation plays in the disease," says Dr. Sharifzadeh. "The findings could help determine whether this approach should be studied further and add to our understanding of the foundational biological mechanisms in Parkinson's disease."
The research is supported by the Innovation in Aging Award from Mayo Clinic's Center for Clinical and Translational Science (CCaTS), the Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging (RAKCA), and the Ida C. & Morris Falk Foundation.
